questions.title: Parametric oscillations of a spring–string pendulum
questions.summary: Find the vertical period T of a mass on a spring, tie a string so d ≈ gT²/π² (pendulum period = 2T), then time the energy exchange between swinging and bouncing. Test t² = km² with two masses.

xlsx.desc: Sample readings for m = 300 g and 400 g with the k = t²/m² comparison.

questions.title: NTC thermistor: resistance and self-heating
questions.summary: Measure the thermistor's resistance at room temperature and in hot water, then analyse a dataset in which the thermistor heats itself as the current rises: R against I, power, and the energy dissipated (area under P–t).

xlsx.desc: A practice version of Q2dataset: t, V and I every 30 s as the e.m.f. is raised. Compute R and P, plot R against I and integrate P over time.

questions.title: Equilibrium of a rod on a pivot and pulley
questions.summary: A rod hinged at its right eye is held horizontal by a string over a pulley. Moving mass Q changes where P must sit; plot τ_Q against τ_P (gradient B ≈ −1, intercept A) and find the rod's weight R = F sin θ − 2A/S; plan an oscillation experiment.

xlsx.desc: Six (q, p) balance positions. Compute τ_P and τ_Q, plot τ_Q against τ_P, and find A, B and R.

2.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="509.7" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">300 g  (0.300 kg)</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="222.0" y="604.5" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Time for 20 oscillations: 13.63 s, 13.71 s</text><text x="222.0" y="616.9" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">mean = 13.67 s   T = mean/20</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="664.7" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">0.684 s</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Even a "record m" line deserves a unit (and it is the value written on the masses: 300 g).
T ≈ 0.7 s is short, so time 20 oscillations (≥ 10 s total) twice. Start the count at "zero" as the mass passes the equilibrium point.
Give T to the precision of t/20, e.g. 0.689 s. Do not round it to 0.7 s.

3.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="185.0" y="170.0" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">l = gT²/π² = 9.81 × (0.684)² / π²</text><text x="185.0" y="183.0" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">   = 0.4644 m</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="212.5" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">0.464 m  (46.4 cm)</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="222.0" y="659.0" font-size="9" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">measured with a metre rule from the top of the string</text><text x="222.0" y="670.7" font-size="9" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">to the centre of the slotted masses</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="683.0" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">46.6 cm</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Why this l: a pendulum of length l = gT²/π² has period 2π√(l/g) = 2T, exactly twice the bounce period. That 2:1 tuning is what makes the parametric energy exchange happen.
Keep l to 3 s.f. (same as T). You need it in cm to tie the knot.
Locate the centre of the masses with a set square against the rule. d is to the centre, not the bottom.

4.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="141.0" y="217.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Released, timed from one "still coils" moment to the next:</text><text x="141.0" y="229.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">t = 22.7 s (repeat: 23.3 s, mean ≈ 23.0 s)</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="266.1" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">22.7 s</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="141.0" y="345.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Judging the instant the coils look stationary: Δt ≈ 1 s</text><text x="141.0" y="357.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">% uncertainty = 1/22.7 × 100%</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="398.1" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">4%</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="141.0" y="495.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">20 oscillations: 15.73 s, 15.77 s</text><text x="141.0" y="507.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">l = 9.81 × (0.787)²/π²</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="626.6" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">400 g</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="651.8" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">0.787 s</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="677.4" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">0.616 m</text></g></svg>

notes.text: The interval is long (≈ 20–30 s) and the moment is a judgement, so the uncertainty is reaction/judgement, not stopwatch precision (0.01 s).
Realistic Δt here is about 1 s. Quoting ±0.01 s or ±0.2 s (reaction time only) understates it.

5.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="266.3" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">61.4 cm</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="291.8" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">30.1 s</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="141.0" y="440.0" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">k = t²/m²</text><text x="141.0" y="453.0" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">k₁ = (22.7)² / (0.300)² = 5725</text><text x="141.0" y="466.0" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">k₂ = (30.1)² / (0.400)² = 5663</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="615.3" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">5700 s² kg⁻²</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="410.0" y="640.5" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">5700 s² kg⁻²</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Give k to 2 s.f. (t is only good to about 4%). Include the unit s² kg⁻².

6.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="160.0" y="129.5" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Percentage difference between k values = |5725 − 5663| / 5663 × 100% =</text><text x="160.0" y="141.7" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">1.1%.</text><text x="160.0" y="156.9" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Since k ∝ t², the uncertainty in k is about 2 × 4% = 9%.</text><text x="160.0" y="172.1" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">1.1% is less than 9%, so the results support t² = km².</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Always compare like with like: % difference in k against the % uncertainty in k (doubled, because t is squared).
Two data points can only "support" a relationship; they cannot prove it.

8.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="411.2" y="147.3" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">26.0 °C</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="411.2" y="400.5" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">0.155 mA</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="411.2" y="425.9" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">1.48 V</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="141.0" y="487.5" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">R = V/I = 1.48 / 1.547×10⁻4</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="411.2" y="534.6" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">9.57 kΩ</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Thermometer reading to 0.5 °C or 1 °C (whatever the scale allows), with the bulb in air away from your hand.
Record meter readings with all the digits shown and the unit (mA, V).
Keep the switch closed only briefly: the current heats the thermistor and lowers R.

9.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="411.2" y="206.6" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">64.5 °C</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="411.2" y="232.0" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">1.47 V</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="411.2" y="257.9" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">0.692 mA</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="141.0" y="345.5" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">R = 1.47 / 6.925×10⁻4 A</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="411.2" y="390.2" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">2.12 kΩ</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Stir and wait for the thermometer and thermistor readings to steady before recording. The water is cooling the whole time.
Check the trend: an NTC thermistor's R must be much smaller in hot water than at room temperature.

11.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="161.0" y="146.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">The thermistor cannot lose heat to the surroundings, so for the same current</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="161.0" y="171.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">its temperature rises higher. Its resistance therefore falls further (R drops</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="161.0" y="196.7" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">more steeply with I). The current for a given e.m.f. becomes larger, which</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="161.0" y="221.7" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">heats it more (positive feedback): the temperature and current may keep</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="161.0" y="246.9" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">rising (thermal runaway) and could damage the thermistor.</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Two marks: link insulation → higher temperature → lower R → larger current/more heating.

17.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q3"><text x="107.0" y="74.5" font-size="9" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Procedure • Keep the hanger mass, pulley height, stand separation and the masses R and</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q3"><text x="107.0" y="100.0" font-size="9" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Q fixed. Place R and Q at chosen distances r and q from the right eye, re-adjusting the</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q3"><text x="107.0" y="125.0" font-size="9" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">hanger load so the rod is horizontal at equilibrium (check with a spirit level). • Displace the</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q3"><text x="107.0" y="150.0" font-size="9" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">mass hanger down by a small fixed amount (about 1 cm) and release. notes.text: Name the graph explicitly and say how A and B come out of it: y-intercept and gradient.
The equilibrium position must be re-established each time R/Q move, otherwise θ and the tension change too.
